transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been going on that brought you in today?

I’m here because I can’t stop thinking about my face. The left side looks crooked to me, like it’s messed up somehow. I know people tell me they don’t see anything, but when I’m at the warehouse or even at salsa night, I feel like everyone’s noticing it. It’s been really hard to get it out of my head.
How long have you been feeling this way about your face, and has it affected your ability to work or enjoy activities like salsa night?

It’s been going on long enough that it’s really messing with things. At work, I’ve been written up because I get delayed, like I can’t just keep moving normally. And yeah, I’ve started skipping stuff I used to like—soccer, salsa nights, even family gatherings—because I don’t want people looking at me or taking pictures.
Do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly, like checking mirrors, touching your face, or comparing it to others, to try to fix or make sure it looks okay?

Yeah. I check it a lot. Like before I go back out on the inventory floor, I’ll stop in the bathroom and look in the mirror again, fix my cap, rub at that same spot on my face, just trying to make it look right. Sometimes I get stuck doing that longer than I mean to, and then I’m late getting back and my picking numbers fall behind. Then my boss gets on me again.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms of preoccupation with a perceived defect in their face, repetitive behaviors (checking mirrors, adjusting appearance), and significant impairment in work and social functioning strongly align with Body Dysmorphic Disorder.
